measured.how: The page's Measure speed button gave these rates on 5 October 2026 in headless Chromium: about 1.9 million replicates a second with 4 workers for the Poisson experiment, and about 62,000 for the survey workflow with 1,000 draws in each replicate. With the main thread 4 times slower, as on an ordinary laptop, the main thread alone gives 211,000 and 4,300. Thus a run of 2^22 replicates of a light model takes about 10 s on an ordinary laptop, and the time limit pauses a longer run. On 6 October 2026 the same button measured the group 3 models: about 1.1 million replicates a second with the workers for a Pareto experiment, and about 105,000 for the slowest workflow, a censored trial with 100 patients and Kaplan–Meier estimates in each replicate (7,600 on the slowed main thread). Its default size of 2^13 thus takes about 1 s on an ordinary laptop, so the published limits hold. On 6 October 2026 the same button measured the group 5 models in headless Chromium. A Brownian path of 16 steps runs about 1.1 million replicates a second with 4 workers, a Clayton copula 1.4 million, and a t copula 860,000. Paths of 250 steps (a compound Poisson surplus, a Markov chain) run about 105,000 to 124,000 a second with the workers and 10,000 on the slowed main thread. A Brownian path at the limit of 4,096 steps with coarsen = 4 (16,384 draws) runs about 2,000 a second with the workers. So its 2^16 replicates take about 33 s, and a larger run reaches the time limit and pauses. Thus a path has at most 4,096 steps, a replicate at most about 20,000 path and copula draws, and a copula at most 16 dimensions.

rare.how: Measured on 6 October 2026 in headless Chromium with 4 workers: tilting of a sum of 20 claims, 64 replications of 65,536 paths, 0.68 s; direct simulation of the catastrophe test, 16 replications of 16,384 paths, 1.3 s; the cross-entropy method on the catastrophe test, 16 replications of 4,096 paths, 3.9 s; subset simulation of a Pareto II sum, 16 replications of 4,096 paths, 0.21 s. The time of a run grows in proportion to N R, so the largest catastrophe run with the cross-entropy method would take about 4 minutes, and the time limit of 180 s pauses it.

chains.how: Measured on 7 October 2026 in headless Chromium with 4 workers, 32 independent runs each: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on the O-ring model with 2^17 iterations in each chain, 2.7 s with 10 leapfrog steps and 36 s with 200; the sequential sampler with 65,536 particles and 20 moves, 15 s; the particle filter with 16,384 particles over 100 days, 2.4 s; scrambled Sobol points, 2^18 points in 16 dimensions, 1.7 s. An ordinary laptop is about 4 times slower, so the heaviest setting takes about 2.5 minutes, and the time limit of 180 s pauses a longer run.

physics.how: Measured on 7 October 2026 in headless Chromium with 4 workers and the main thread slowed 4 times (the workers ran at full speed): the default examples took 0.6 to 1.7 s each, finite-size scaling up to L = 128 with 2^13 drives in each of 8 chains took 3.4 s, and L = 128 with 2^16 drives in each of 8 chains took 7.1 s. A run of the largest settings, 64 chains of 2^18 drives at L = 128, would take several minutes, so the time limit of 180 s pauses it and marks the result as partial.
